item.title: Liz Truss claims Brits would be on Mars by 2040 if she hadn’t been ousted
item.dc:creator: Noah Keate
item.description: Former prime minister dreams of a brighter alternative future.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON — Liz Truss claims the U.K. would have managed successful missions to Mars within years — if only her 49-day premiership hadn’t been cut short.

The assertion comes in the former British prime minister’s new book “Bank Job,” which was published Monday and claims to explain “how the Bank of England broke the bond market and brought down the government” when her mini-budget in 2022 precipitated market turmoil.

In its closing chapter, the book paints a vivid picture of what Truss believes life in 2040 would be like if her policies had been given a chance to bed in. “Several missions to Mars have now been launched from Britain’s space port,” Truss’ book imagines.

The ex-PM also opts for some more grounded policy dreams.

She envisages a 2040 in which “there are now no European Union laws in Britain,” a “permissive regime for artificial intelligence” is in place, and tumbling energy costs and faster planning timelines have helped make the U.K. a leader in AI.

“Bitcoin received tax treatment consistent with its status as a form of money for commercial purposes,” she imagines. “No central bank digital currency was introduced.”

Since leaving office after a revolt in her own party, Truss has dismissed claims her economic decisions — which included a huge energy bills bailout and tax cuts funded by fresh borrowing — were responsible for crashing the pound.

She has instead pointed the finger at the central bank, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility watchdog, accusing them of working against her. Her new book takes direct aim at the Bank of England, which proposed to sell £80 billion of gilts before the mini-budget, although delayed that sale amid market turmoil.

Truss lost her House of Commons seat at the 2024 general election, and has since been involved in launching the Conservative Political Action Conference in Britain.

item.title: Burnham wants UK back in EU within his lifetime
item.dc:creator: Noah Keate
item.description: But British prime minister rules out rejoin push in current parliament.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Monday his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.

Asked by ITV’s Good Morning Britain Monday whether he wanted to rejoin the EU, Burnham said: “I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime, I would like to see that happen but I am not going to move ahead of the public.

“I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the public, the British public, are the bosses.”

At the ruling Labour Party’s conference last month, Burnham called for closer links with the EU.

He has yet to spell out precise details of the relationship he would seek — but the party’s 2024 election-winning manifesto under Keir Starmer ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or accepting freedom of movement with the bloc.

Burnham said Monday that the promises of the 2016 referendum that took Britain out of the EU have not been delivered.

“We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign,” he said. “It’s weakened our economy. It’s also weakened our control of immigration and that might surprise people.”

But he said: “I’m not proposing rejoining in this Parliament. We’re way, way away from that at this particular moment in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better than the arrangement we’ve got right now.”

The PM’s remarks come after he told the Sunday Times that accepting freedom of movement with the bloc should not be off the table in future negotiations.

A U.K.-EU summit is scheduled for next month, although that is set to focus tightly on technical tweaks to the existing relationship rather than addressing bigger questions of Britain’s future ties to the bloc.

item.title: Cyberangriffe kommen nicht nur zu Bürozeiten
item.dc:creator: Vodafone
item.description: Künstliche Intelligenz verschärft die Bedrohungslage für Unternehmen und stellt klassische Schutzkonzepte auf die Probe. Wie sich IT-Systeme dennoch wirksam und rund um die Uhr schützen lassen, zeigt Babor mit innovativen Sicherheitslösungen.
item.content:encoded:
An diesem Vormittag wartet die IT-Abteilung von Babor auf einen Cyberangriff. Genauer gesagt auf das Ergebnis eines Cyberangriffs, den sie selbst in Auftrag gegeben hat: Ein Penetrationstest soll zeigen, wie gut die Systeme des Kosmetikherstellers geschützt sind. Denn die Bedrohungslage verändert sich. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie Unternehmen arbeiten, sondern auch, wie sie angegriffen werden. Phishing-Mails lassen sich heute in Sekunden auf ihre Opfer zuschneiden, Schadsoftware kann sich automatisiert an Abwehrmechanismen anpassen, und Angriffsmuster entwickeln sich schneller weiter, als klassische Sicherheitskonzepte nachziehen können. Für Unternehmen werden damit zwei Fragen immer wichtiger: Wie schnell erkennen sie einen Angriff und wie reagieren sie darauf?

Ein Härtetest für die IT-Sicherheit

Gemeinsam mit den Expertinnen und Experten von Vodafone und SITS hat das Team die eigene IT-Infrastruktur einem kontrollierten Cyberangriff ausgesetzt. Die Frage ist, wie gut die Systeme einem echten Angreifer standhalten würden und vor allem, wie früh ein solcher Angriff erkannt wird. „Das Ergebnis haben wir mit Spannung erwartet“, sagt Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor. Für die IT-Abteilung ist der Test mehr als eine technische Übung. Babor betreibt rund 200 Server am Hauptsitz in Aachen, dazu kommen weitere Rechenzentrumsstrukturen an unterschiedlichen Standorten. ERP-Systeme, Datenbanken und Kollaborationstools bilden die Grundlage der täglichen Geschäftsprozesse. Weltweit vernetzte Standorte mit Tochtergesellschaften in Europa und Nordamerika sowie mehr als 1000 Mitarbeitern machen die Infrastruktur zusätzlich komplex. Entsprechend hoch sind die Anforderungen an ihre Absicherung. Die bisher eingesetzte Sicherheitslösung stieß zunehmend an ihre Grenzen. Gesucht war ein Ansatz, der nicht nur automatisiert auf verdächtige Aktivitäten reagiert, sondern die gesamte Infrastruktur rund um die Uhr im Blick behält und bei Bedarf Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten hinzuzieht. Inzwischen ist ein solches Security Operations Center (SOC) bei Babor im Einsatz. Der Penetrationstest sollte deshalb auch zeigen, wie gut die neue Sicherheitsarchitektur im Ernstfall funktioniert.

Der Moment der Wahrheit

Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.

Endlich liegen die Ergebnisse des Tests auf dem Tisch. Die Anspannung weicht der Erleichterung. „Wir waren dann aber ein Stück weit beruhigt: Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.“ Der Test zeigt damit zweierlei: Die vorhandenen Schutzmechanismen greifen und das Zusammenspiel aus automatisierter Erkennung und der Analyse durch Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten funktioniert. Gleichzeitig wird deutlich, dass IT-Sicherheit eine Aufgabe ist, die kontinuierliche Aufmerksamkeit erfordert. Denn ein Angriff hält sich nicht an Bürozeiten, und eine IT-Abteilung kann nicht rund um die Uhr vor den Bildschirmen sitzen.

Die Lösung: Security Operations Center

Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Das externe Security Operations Center übernimmt für Babor die kontinuierliche Überwachung der IT-Infrastruktur und kombiniert automatisierte Prozesse mit der Analyse durch erfahrene Security Expertinnen oder -Experten. Sicherheitsrelevante Ereignisse werden fortlaufend analysiert, Auffälligkeiten bewertet und bei Bedarf entsprechende Maßnahmen eingeleitet. Für die interne IT bedeutet das eine zusätzliche Sicherheitsebene und zugleich mehr Freiraum für andere Aufgaben. Statt sämtliche sicherheitsrelevanten Ereignisse selbst rund um die Uhr überwachen und einordnen zu müssen, kann das Babor-Team auf die Expertise der SOC-Spezialisten zurückgreifen. Auch Anforderungen, die über den reinen Schutz der IT-Systeme hinausgehen, lassen sich auf diese Weise berücksichtigen. Dazu zählen etwa Vorgaben aus dem Bereich Compliance oder Anforderungen der Cyberversicherung. Das SOC schafft damit eine Struktur, in der Sicherheitsereignisse kontinuierlich beobachtet und nach definierten Prozessen bearbeitet werden können. Für Rüdiger Mohnen, IT Leiter von Babor, macht sich die Unterstützung bereits im Arbeitsalltag bemerkbar: „Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns voll auf unser Kerngeschäft konzentrieren können. Wir wissen, dass unser Firmennetz durch eine zusätzliche Instanz zuverlässig geschützt ist und haben im Ernstfall jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite. Für mittelständische Unternehmen ist der Verzicht auf ein SOC aus meiner Sicht fahrlässig.“ Der Cyberangriff an diesem Vormittag war kontrolliert. Die nächste Attacke wird es möglicherweise nicht sein. Für Babor kommt es deshalb darauf an, Bedrohungen nicht erst dann zu erkennen, wenn sie Schaden angerichtet haben. Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Eine zusätzliche Schutzinstanz

Drei Fragen an Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor, und Rüdiger Mohnen, IT-Leiter von Babor.

Warum setzt Babor beim Schutz seines Firmennetzes auf ein externes Security Operations Center?

Mirella Fiebes: Für uns war entscheidend, ein durchgängiges 24/7-Monitoring sicherzustellen. Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Rüdiger Mohnen: Zuverlässiger Cyberschutz ist für uns essenziell – nicht zuletzt im Hinblick auf Compliance-Anforderungen und die Vorgaben unserer Cyberversicherung. Ausfälle infolge von Cyberangriffen würden schnell erhebliche Kosten verursachen.

Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Welche konkreten Vorteile bringt Ihnen das SOC?

Rüdiger Mohnen: Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns konsequent auf unser Kerngeschäft fokussieren können. Gleichzeitig gewinnen wir zusätzliche Sicherheit durch eine unabhängige Instanz sowie durch die enge Zusammenarbeit mit den Security-Expert:innen. Im Ernstfall haben wir jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite.

Warum haben Sie sich für Vodafone Business als Partner entschieden?

Mirella Fiebes: Das Angebot von Vodafone hat uns inhaltlich und konzeptionell überzeugt. Diese Entscheidung wurde sowohl in der Implementierungsphase – gemeinsam mit dem Partner SITS – als auch im laufenden Betrieb bestätigt.

Lesen Sie auch dieses spannende Praxisbeispiel: Wie gelingt wirksame Cybersicherheit im Mittelstand? Gewinnen Sie Einblicke in die Sicherheitsstrategie der NXTGN Solutions GmbH und erfahren Sie, wie sich das Unternehmen gegen moderne Cyberbedrohungen wappnet: mehr erfahren und Video ansehen.

Lesen Sie weitere Erfolgsgeschichten von Unternehmen in Zusammenarbeit mit Vodafone Business auf www.vodafone.de

item.title: Trump on Norway: ‘Shithouse country’
item.dc:creator: Ali Walker, Jalen Beckford
item.description: "What about me?" wonders U.S. president in a new blast at Oslo over the Nobel Peace Prize.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump on Sunday night said Norway “sucks,” as he fulminated about being repeatedly overlooked for the Nobel Peace Prize.

Despite starting a war with Iran and toppling the leader of Venezuela, Trump has vigorously touted his peacemaking credentials, claiming to have settled at least eight conflicts during his second term in office.  

But he was passed over twice by the Oslo-based Nobel committee: in 2025 for María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition figurehead; and in 2026 for South African jurist Navi Pillay, for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

“What about me? Do they do two of them? So I’m not in love with Norway. Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” the U.S. president mused during a campaign rally speech in Port Huron, Michigan.

Trump was railing about immigration to the U.S. when he segued into the criticism of Norway.

“We work with Denmark, good country, good nice country. Anybody that would like to come into our country from Denmark, I’m all for it. But I must tell you, from Somalia … I’ve had it with them. I’ve had it with them. I much prefer Denmark. Denmark, we’ll take them. Sweden, Norway … I don’t think so because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize even though I ended it. So I don’t want anybody from Norway. I don’t want anything to do with Norway,” Trump said.

Espen Barth Eide, Norway’s foreign minister, responded to Trump’s remarks by reiterating the Nobel committee’s independence. “He knows very well that the Nobel committee is independent. We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering, and that is still the case,” Eide told Norwegian news outlet NRK Monday.

While Trump didn’t get the 2025 prize, the Venezuelan winner did present him with her medal during a meeting at the White House in January this year.

“And the person who got it, Maria, was very nice,” the president said during his rally speech. “She said, ‘I can’t believe I got it. This should go to President Trump,’ and she gave me her Nobel Peace Prize, that was so nice. It was very nice. I won’t forget that. It was very nice.”

item.title: French presidential hopeful Philippe slips in new poll
item.dc:creator: Pauline de Saint Remy
item.description: The former PM lost three points compared to Cluster 17’s survey from last month.
item.content:encoded:
PARIS — Former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe is losing ground to far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the French presidential race, according to polling conducted exclusively for POLITICO.

The survey, carried out by Cluster 17 between Oct. 19 and Oct. 22, showed Philippe with 16% trailing Mélenchon on 18.5%. Cluster 17’s poll on the presidential election last month had the two tied at 19% apiece.

Both leaders are significantly behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, who held her first presidential campaign rally on Sunday. Le Pen’s candidacy does not appear to have been significantly affected by allegations that her protégé Jordan Bardella made antisemitic comments in private as a teenager. Bardella, who was reelected as president of the National Rally at the far-right party’s conference this past weekend, has repeatedly denied the accusations.

Philippe’s main ideological rival, fellow former PM Gabriel Attal, fares little better in the poll. When tested instead of Philippe as the main centrist candidate, Attal netted just 12%.

Raphaël Glucksmann, fresh off his dominant victory in a center-left primary, is holding steady at fourth place with 13% in Cluster 17’s survey. The pollster found Glucksmann would net 29% of those who supported President Emmanuel Macron in 2022, while 49% of those voters back Philippe. Macron cannot run for a third consecutive term.

Conservative leader Bruno Retailleau is still struggling to break into double digits. Though he held steady in the poll, he has a new cause for concern: the rising popularity of David Lisnard, the right-wing mayor of Cannes.

In a scenario in which Lisnard is added to the race, he eclipses Retailleau and also chips away at support for Le Pen.

A poll unveiled last week found little change in the dynamics of the race following the rioting that emerged on the sidelines of massive protests across France on Oct. 17. Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets again on Saturday.

item.title: 4 reasons Andy Burnham’s MPs are feeling more cheerful — and the pitfalls ahead
item.dc:creator: Noah Keate, Isabel Loubser
item.description: The British PM's party is impressed with his first 100 days but warn hurdles ahead could test that goodwill.
item.content:encoded:
LONDON — Andy Burnham pledged to bring back hope when he entered Downing Street. Labour MPs are feeling it — for now.

The British prime minister is approaching 100 days in No. 10 this week with his party believing things are on the up.

Keir Starmer was toppled earlier this year after disastrous local election results precipitated a loss of confidence in his administration.

Disgruntled Labour MPs warned their new leader must show up, listen to them and accept some disagreement to avoid repeating his predecessor’s mistakes.

POLITICO sets out the four reasons Labour MPs are feeling more chipper under Burnham — but they still see potential pitfalls ahead.

Some of the dozen parliamentarians interviewed by POLITICO for this piece were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the internal party matters.

1) Disagreement is tolerated

MPs reckon Burnham’s administration is more willing to recognize different views within the broad church Labour Party.

Burnham himself told a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting that disagreement is fine as long as MPs speak to him about it, according to Simon Opher — a 2024-intake MP and member of Mainstream, the soft-left faction supported by Burnham when he was Greater Manchester mayor.

“It sounds weird, but that is a remarkable difference from what they had before,” Opher said, claiming he felt a “slight climate of fear” early in his political career.

Starmer infuriated MPs when weeks after taking office he suspended the whip from those who voted to scrap a two-child benefit cap — only to U-turn earlier this year.

By contrast, Kim Johnson, a member of Labour’s left-wing Socialist Campaign Group faction, points out she wasn’t sanctioned after abstaining on the government’s Courts and Tribunals Bill earlier this month because she believes it still weakens the right to trial by jury.

“You’re not feeling you can’t do that or risk losing the whip,” she said.

Of course, Burnham’s appetite for disagreement hasn’t been fully put to the test.

He entered No. 10 at the start of the summer recess, when MPs were away from Westminster, and there was a month-long conference recess when they returned to SW1 in September.

And MPs don’t want a totally laissez-faire regime.

“I didn’t get into politics to sit in a room and just agree with each other,” said another 2024-intake Labour MP. “I don’t think you get good policy by just sitting around like nodding dogs.”

But they said they “genuinely believe in collective responsibility,” and are “quite relaxed” about the consequences of voting against the whip.

Another backbench MP warns Burnham’s lax approach can only last so long.

“Andy is riding high still, he is not in [Nigel] Farage or [Zack] Polanski territory, he can afford for people to go ‘I don’t like this.’ It’s when the shit hits the fan, and the public are saying they’re not happy, then you begin to find the political patience wears out,” that backbencher added.

Burnham may yet regret his promise that the whips office will act as an HR department, the MP said, “because you want them to come down like a clonking fist.”

2) Ministers are more visible

Burnham’s team is making itself seen, his MPs report.

Whips have been calling them to check in, and Burnham himself has attended PLP sub-group meetings. Cabinet ministers have also been available for meetings.

Though another Socialist Campaign Group MP admitted “it’s a very low bar” for improvement. “Under Starmer, there was very little in terms of consultations, any discussions about anything at all.”

Mainstream member Alex Sobel said: “I’ve had more meetings with No. 10 — I’ve been to No. 10 North — in these three months than the entire time of the previous administration.”

Bill Esterson, who chairs the Energy Security Committee, said he had “regular conversations with No. 10” and that Burnham’s team had “engaged very fully” with committee chairs and the PLP more broadly.

A second 2024 intake MP said: “There’s definitely more of a concerted attempt for them to be reaching out and listening to us.” The days of being viewed “as the legal necessity to get legislation through” are over.

3) Burnham’s political instincts

MPs reckon they’ve had an upgrade when it comes to raw political instincts.

“There’s a feeling that we’ve got a guy up front who we can get behind,” said Opher.

“He understands how politics works,” he added, citing the decision to delay approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field until after the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Labour faced a challenge from the Greens. “Andy’s much more savvy on what he’s doing.”

Backbenchers also claim to feel more confident they won’t get caught in the Starmer flip-flop policy trap.

The unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP quoted above is still smarting over the “absolutely awful” two-child benefit cap vote, where rebels lost the whip only for it later to become government policy.

The first 2024-intake MP reckons Burnham is better able to communicate difficult trade-offs, like altering the triple lock to fund social care.

4) Voters are giving Labour another chance

It is ultimately Burnham’s popularity with the public that has fed into the positive mood.

Many Labour MPs “agreed with the punters on the doorstep” about Starmer’s inadequacies, Opher said. Data showing Labour has retaken the opinion poll lead from Reform UK has boosted their optimism. “It doesn’t feel like a party that is about to be ripped apart,” he added.

The first 2024 intake MP said: “It has given us the right to be heard,” said the first 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above. “People feel warmly towards Andy, which is half the battle. I think they trust his good intentions.”

Some flashpoints ahead…

1) The budget

Burnham can only coast on the good vibes for so long, and the first test of tough political choices comes Wednesday in the budget.

MPs on the left see the economic statement as a “crunch point” that will show if the chancellor will put his money where the PM’s mouth is.

“If there’s an attempt to take money from ordinary people who’ve got nothing and no attempt to get finances from people who have got far too much, then probably there will be some sort of opposition”, said the unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted. They hope to see the already trailed bank tax confirmed, or a wealth tax.

They warned that any decisions on what to cut and where to spend will pose “challenges from both sides of the PLP.”

“The measure of Andy Burnham is how he deals with it,” they added.

2) Welfare

Burnham wants to avoid a repeat of the botched attempt at welfare reform which severely weakened Starmer’s authority.

A long-awaited review by former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs) will be published shortly with recommendations.

Milburn — alongside Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden — has been trying to ensure communication is better.

“Pat has done an excellent job at building a consensus, rolling the carpet, setting out the argument, setting out the moral case, but he was doing that before the change of administration,” a third 2024-intake Labour MP said.

The second 2024 Labour MP quoted above said most colleagues “feel like it’s a decent stab at it and it’s not come out of the blue.” Reasonable critics “were just getting stonewalled” last year.

Esterson, who’s served in parliament since 2010, said regular engagement means “it’s not surprising that you get the benefit of the doubt far more often than if you don’t.”

3) Europe

Burnham’s admission that a future Labour manifesto could commit to a referendum on EU membership is already opening old Brexit wounds — and not in the way Labour wants.

The Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted is uneasy about its potential to spark further division. “It nearly ripped the country apart and I’m not sure if it’s the right thing to do [to] reignite that horribleness in each constituency,” they said.

The third 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above concurred. While people want a closer relationship with Europe, they believe rejoining is a “different kettle of fish” and jars with constituents who want “better public services and more economic growth” rather than continental renegotiations.

4) Energy

Energy policy has already become a flashpoint. The decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field was met with some dissent. A decision about the larger Rosebank oil and gas field is still looming.

Sobel told POLITICO’s London Playbook it “won’t make an impact on global prices and will give mixed messages in terms of investment in terms of both renewables and decarbonisation of home heating.”

Left-wing Labour MPs also signed a letter to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh urging her to reject the licenses due to climate change. “Every second we continue pumping fossil fuels into the atmosphere makes the crisis more severe,” the letter organized by Chris Hinchliff said.

The second 2024-intake MP quoted thought ministers are acting in good faith.

“They’ve got one go at government and they seem to be doing their absolute best to give it a good whack,” they said.

Sam Blewett contributed reporting.

item.title: SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. La chute de Philippe, relégué derrière Mélenchon
item.dc:creator: Pauline de Saint Remy
item.description: SONDAGE CLUSTER 17 x POLITICO. L'ancien Premier ministre chute de 3 points par rapport à notre enquête précédente, tandis que Jean-Luc Mélenchon reste haut et Marine Le Pen monte.
item.content:encoded:
Mauvaise nouvelle pour Edouard Philippe : l’ancien Premier ministre n’avait déjà pas réussi à enclencher une dynamique dans sa campagne, il chute désormais dans les intentions de vote et se classe bon troisième, derrière Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Le maire du Havre perd 3 points dans une nouvelle enquête réalisée par l’institut Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, du 19 au 20 octobre, passant de 19% à 16% des intentions de vote, par comparaison avec notre étude précédente réalisée les 15 et 16 septembre. Il est désormais nettement devancé par Jean-Luc Mélenchon, qui, lui, est quasiment stable à 18,5% (-0,5).

A ce stade de la campagne, l’Insoumis est donc le mieux placé pour se qualifier pour le second tour face à Marine Le Pen, quelles que soient les configurations.

La candidate du RN, elle, ne pâtit manifestement pas de la révélation par Mediapart fin septembre d’anciens écrits antisémites attribués à Jordan Bardella, et reste hyperfavorite du premier tour, avec 33% d’intentions de vote lorsque Philippe représente le bloc central, contre 31% dans notre dernière enquête.

A noter : fraîchement auréolé de sa victoire dès le premier round à la primaire du PS et de Place publique, Raphaël Glucksmann, lui, passe de 12% à 13% des intentions de vote, en légère dynamique. Dans le détail, selon Cluster 17, le social-démocrate récolterait 29% des voix des électeurs d’Emmanuel Macron en 2022, ce qui explique en partie pourquoi seuls 49% d’entre eux voteraient Philippe.

“Glucksmann progresse parce que Philippe ne s’adresse pas assez à l’aile sociale-démocrate de l’espace modéré”, note Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de Cluster 17.

Retailleau doublé par Lisnard

Quant au candidat des Républicains, Bruno Retailleau, il ne décolle toujours pas, mais se maintient avec 7,5%-8% des intentions de vote. Il a toutefois une nouvelle raison de s’inquiéter : lorsque David Lisnard, étiqueté Nouvelle Energie, est testé lui aussi, il atteint les 8%, grappillant des points à Le Pen (30,5%), Retailleau (7%), ainsi qu’Eric Zemmour (qui passe de 4% à 3,5%).

La cote du maire de Cannes, pourtant encore méconnu d’une partie des Français, s’explique parce qu’il “répond à une forte demande de libéralisme du centre et même de miléisme des très conservateurs”, commente Jean-Yves Dormagen, en référence au président argentin Javier Milei.

Testée également par Cluster 17, l’hypothèse d’une candidature de Gabriel Attal à la place de celle d’Edouard Philippe ne donnera guère plus d’espoir aux partisans du bloc central : le secrétaire général de Renaissance recueillerait 12% des voix aujourd’hui, contre 13,5% selon le même institut au mois de septembre. Dans ce scénario, Jean-Luc Mélenchon grimperait lui à 19,5% et Raphaël Glucksmann à 14%.

(*) Sondage réalisé du 19 au 22 octobre auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française âgée de 18 ans et plus grâce à la méthode des quotas. L’enquête a été réalisée via un questionnaire autoadministré en ligne. La marge d’erreur est comprise entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.
